```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r libraries}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidytext)
library(quanteda)
library(tibble)
```

```{r load-texts}
hw_dir <- "C:/Users/titin/OneDrive - Duke University/TAD/HW2/"

com_file   <- paste0(hw_dir, "A07594__Circle_of_Commerce.txt")
trade_file <- paste0(hw_dir, "B14801__Free_Trade.txt")
file_c     <- paste0(hw_dir, "A06785.txt")

com_txt   <- read_file(com_file)
trade_txt <- read_file(trade_file)
text_c    <- read_file(file_c)

texts <- tibble(
  doc_title = c("Commerce Text", "Trade Text", "Text C"),
  text = c(com_txt, trade_txt, text_c)
)

texts
```

```{r stopword-lists}
# Standard tidytext stopword list, as in Week 02
data("stop_words")
```


## Part I: Raw-Count Sentiment Analysis

### Step 1: Tokenize and clean the text

One cleaned set of tokens is created for all three documents. These same tokens are used for both the raw-count analysis (Part I) and the TF-IDF analysis (Part II).

```{r tokenize-clean}
words_clean <- texts %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  mutate(
    word = str_to_lower(word),
    word = str_replace_all(word, "ſ", "s")   # normalize the long s
  ) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

words_clean
```

### Step 2: Join tokens to the Bing sentiment dictionary

```{r bing-join}
bing <- get_sentiments("bing")

# Only the Commerce and Trade texts are analyzed for sentiment
words_sentiment <- words_clean %>%
  filter(doc_title %in% c("Commerce Text", "Trade Text")) %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word")

words_sentiment
```

### Step 3: Compute raw sentiment totals

```{r raw-sentiment}
raw_sentiment <- words_sentiment %>%
  count(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  rename(raw_positive = positive, raw_negative = negative) %>%
  mutate(raw_net = raw_positive - raw_negative)

raw_sentiment
```


## Part II: TF-IDF-Weighted Sentiment Analysis

### Step 4: Compute TF-IDF for words in each document

The DFM is built directly from the cleaned tidy tokens from Step 1 (`cast_dfm()`), so the text-cleaning decisions are identical across both analyses. All three documents are included so that IDF is calculated over the full corpus.

```{r tfidf}
corpus_dfm <- words_clean %>%
  count(doc_title, word) %>%
  cast_dfm(doc_title, word, n)

corpus_dfm

corpus_tfidf <- dfm_tfidf(corpus_dfm)
```

### Step 5: Convert the TF-IDF results to a tidy table

```{r tfidf-tidy}
tfidf_tidy <- convert(corpus_tfidf, to = "data.frame") %>%
  rename(doc_title = doc_id) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -doc_title,
    names_to = "word",
    values_to = "tfidf"
  ) %>%
  filter(tfidf > 0) %>%
  # Text C was only needed to calculate IDF
  filter(doc_title %in% c("Commerce Text", "Trade Text"))

tfidf_tidy %>%
  arrange(desc(tfidf))
```

### Step 6: Keep only sentiment-bearing words

```{r tfidf-sentiment}
tfidf_sentiment <- tfidf_tidy %>%
  inner_join(bing, by = "word")

top_tfidf_sentiment <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  slice_max(tfidf, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(doc_title, sentiment, desc(tfidf))

print(top_tfidf_sentiment, n = Inf)
```

### Step 7: Compute TF-IDF-weighted sentiment totals

```{r tfidf-totals}
tfidf_totals <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  summarise(weight = sum(tfidf), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sentiment,
    values_from = weight,
    values_fill = 0
  ) %>%
  rename(tfidf_positive = positive, tfidf_negative = negative) %>%
  mutate(tfidf_net = tfidf_positive - tfidf_negative)

tfidf_totals
```


## Part III: Compare Raw vs. TF-IDF Sentiment

```{r comparison}
sentiment_comparison <- raw_sentiment %>%
  left_join(tfidf_totals, by = "doc_title") %>%
  select(doc_title,
         raw_positive, raw_negative, raw_net,
         tfidf_positive, tfidf_negative, tfidf_net)

print(sentiment_comparison, width = Inf)

write_csv(sentiment_comparison, paste0(hw_dir, "sentiment_comparison.csv"))
```

The most frequent sentiment words under raw counts (used for Question 3):

```{r top-raw-words}
top_raw_words <- words_sentiment %>%
  count(doc_title, sentiment, word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  group_by(doc_title, sentiment) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  ungroup()

print(top_raw_words, n = Inf)
```


## Part IV: Interpretive Questions

**1. What changed between the two methods?**

Under raw counts, both texts look positive. The Commerce Text has 491 positive and 423 negative words (net +68), and the Trade Text has 344 positive and 281 negative words (net +63). After TF-IDF weighting, the sign flips for both texts and both become net negative. The Commerce Text scores 63.0 positive and 86.3 negative (net −23.3), and the Trade Text scores 32.7 positive and 44.2 negative (net −11.5). The comparison between the two texts also changes. Under raw counts their net scores are almost the same (68 vs. 63), even though the Commerce Text has many more sentiment words (914 vs. 625). Under TF-IDF, the Commerce Text's net score is about twice as negative as the Trade Text's.

**2. Why did TF-IDF alter the results?**

Raw counting gives every occurrence of a Bing word a weight of 1. TF-IDF multiplies each word's count by log10(3 / number of documents containing the word). A sentiment word that appears in all three texts (Circle of Commerce, Free Trade, and A06785) gets an IDF of 0 and disappears from the TF-IDF score, no matter how often it is used. Only words found in one text (IDF ≈ 0.48) or two texts (IDF ≈ 0.18) keep any weight. Many of the most frequent sentiment words are shared across the three texts, because all three are about the same subject (trade, money, and the exchange). Most of the raw positive count was made up of these shared words. Once they are removed, the remaining distinctive vocabulary leans negative. So the TF-IDF score does not tell us that the texts are "really" negative. It tells us that the sentiment words unique to each text are mostly negative ones.

**3. Which specific words drove the changes?**

The most frequent negative words in the Commerce Text under raw counts were *decay* (14), *stranger* (13), *abuse* (12), *fall* (11), *false* (10), and *mystery* (9). None of them appear among the highest TF-IDF words. If they were in only one or two texts, their TF-IDF weight would be large enough to reach the top-10 list, so they must appear in all three documents and carry a weight of 0. The TF-IDF results are instead driven by words that appear only in one text. In the Commerce Text these are negative words such as *impertinent* (2.86), *imperfect* (2.39), and *meddle* (1.91), and positive words such as *passion* (4.29), *divine* (3.34), and *affection* (2.86). In the Trade Text, all five of the highest-weighted sentiment words are negative: *imposition* (3.34), *disorderly* (2.86), *deficient*, *pleas*, and *loose*. They are followed by *confront*, *cruelty*, *extortion*, and *repugnant*. Together with *imposition*, *extortion* points to Free Trade's complaints about taxes and charges on trade rather than to a general negative mood.

Several of these words show the limits of a modern dictionary on 17th-century English. *Stranger* usually means a foreign merchant, and *mystery* means a trade or craft, not something negative. *Imposition* in Free Trade refers to taxes on goods, not to a feeling. *Impertinent* in this period mostly means "irrelevant." *Passion* and *affection* are probably used critically, as in an opponent "led by passion," even though Bing labels them positive. Words like *impertinent*, *imperfect*, and *meddle* fit the polemical tone of the Misselden–Malynes debate rather than a general mood.

**4. When would each method be more appropriate? What limitation does document length create for the raw-count measure?**

Raw counts are more appropriate when the question is about a text's overall tone or how much evaluative language it uses, especially when the documents are of similar length. TF-IDF weighting is more appropriate when the question is what makes a text's evaluative language *distinctive* compared with the rest of the corpus, for example which charged words set one side of the Malynes–Misselden debate apart. TF-IDF needs a reasonably large corpus, though. With only three documents, the IDF can take only three values, so these results should not be taken too seriously. The main limitation of raw counts is document length. The Commerce Text is much longer than the Trade Text (about 34,000 vs. 20,000 tokens in Homework 1), so it has more positive *and* more negative words simply because it has more words. Its raw net score of +68 looks slightly more positive than the Trade Text's +63. As a share of sentiment words, though, the Trade Text is more positive (63 / 625 ≈ 10% vs. 68 / 914 ≈ 7%). Raw net scores should be normalized, for example by total tokens or total sentiment words, before texts of different lengths are compared.


## Challenge Extension: Sentiment Concentration vs. Diffusion

```{r challenge}
total_weight <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title) %>%
  summarise(total_sentiment_weight = sum(tfidf))

top5 <- tfidf_sentiment %>%
  group_by(doc_title) %>%
  slice_max(tfidf, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup()

top5

top5 %>%
  group_by(doc_title) %>%
  summarise(top5_weight = sum(tfidf)) %>%
  left_join(total_weight, by = "doc_title") %>%
  mutate(top5_share = round(top5_weight / total_sentiment_weight, 3))
```

In both texts, sentiment is spread across many words rather than concentrated in a few. The top five words carry only 10.5% of the sentiment weight in the Commerce Text and 13.6% in the Trade Text. The Trade Text is slightly more concentrated, and all five of its top words are negative.
